vignette:
At thirty-six, she is used to working in places where noise is constant and the ground never feels entirely settled. She spends her days on construction sites in a hard hat and steel-toed boots, moving between crews, checking materials, climbing scaffolding without much thought. Before she got sick, she thinks of herself as the one who kept going. She worked through heat, through sore muscles, through long shifts, and then went home to her husband and the ordinary routines of dinner, laundry, sleep. She had always trusted her body to do what she asked of it.

The illness begins in a way she first tries to minimize. She tells herself the fatigue is from overtime. The shortness of breath must be dust, weather, a lingering cold. Even when she starts waking at night with her heart pounding and a pressure in her chest, she delays going in. She is proud of not complaining. On the site, she leans against a stack of drywall one morning, waiting for the dizziness to pass, embarrassed that a younger coworker asks if she is okay.

The day everything changes, she is at work. She remembers the brightness of the sun on poured concrete and the smell of cut wood. Then she remembers the strange feeling that the air has thinned out around her. Her hands go numb. Someone is talking to her, but the words seem far away. She tries to answer and cannot catch her breath. The next clear memory is being lowered onto the ground while voices move quickly above her. She sees faces looking down, her hard hat off, her hair stuck to her forehead. In the ambulance she becomes certain she is dying. She watches the monitor, the oxygen mask, the gloved hands, and thinks not in dramatic words but in practical ones: her husband does not know where she is, the truck is still at the site, she has not paid the electric bill.

In the hospital, the illness becomes real through machines and other people’s expressions. She is told she is seriously ill and may not have come in much later. She does not repeat the details easily now; what stays with her is not one sentence but the feeling of her body becoming something unstable and dangerous. There are nights of alarms, fluorescent lights, and staff rushing in when her numbers change. She lies awake listening to footsteps in the hallway, afraid to fall asleep because each time she closes her eyes she imagines not waking up. When her husband leaves at night, she smiles so he will not see how terrified she is. As soon as he is gone, she watches the door and feels abandoned by the ordinary world.

She survives, but afterward she does not feel returned to her life so much as dropped back into it. At home, everyone expects gratitude and relief. She tries to feel those things. Instead, she startles at every change in her body. A cough can ruin her whole day. If her heart beats too fast after carrying groceries, she is back in the ambulance. She checks her oxygen level, her temperature, her breathing. She studies her face in the mirror for signs she is becoming sick again. Her husband tells her she is okay, but reassurance does not hold for long. She asks him, more than once, whether he thinks she looks pale.

Returning to construction is harder than she expected. The site had once been noisy in a familiar way; now the sounds hit her all at once. The hiss of pneumatic tools, shouted warnings, engines reversing—her body reacts before she can think. When she has to climb, she notices her breath too closely and panic rises fast, hot, and humiliating. She begins finding excuses to stay on the ground, then feels ashamed watching others do work she used to handle easily. If a coworker jokes that she should take it easy, she hears pity in it and grows quiet for the rest of the shift.

At night she dreams in fragments from the hospital: the monitor alarm, the ceiling tiles passing overhead, the sensation of trying to pull air into lungs that will not cooperate. She wakes drenched in sweat, sitting upright, one hand pressed to her chest. Her husband reaches for her and sometimes she lets him, but sometimes she pulls away because she cannot bear to be touched when she feels trapped inside the memory. On those nights she goes to the kitchen, drinks water, and stands in the dark listening to the refrigerator hum until her breathing slows.

She has become careful in ways that make her world smaller. She avoids medical dramas, avoids the road that passes the hospital, avoids talking in detail about what happened at work that day. Family members ask whether she is fully recovered, and she says, “Alhamdulillah, I’m better,” because it is easier than explaining that better is not the same as safe. She still goes to work, still packs her lunch before dawn, still jokes with coworkers when she can. From the outside she appears strong, even stubborn. But much of her day is spent scanning for danger inside her own body, living as if catastrophe is not in the past but just a few breaths away.
